ex:quantum-universe-su2:
Example \mathrm{SU}(2) as a quantum universe. Continuing rigid monoidal Vect, the quantum universe axioms are checked here for G = \mathrm{SU}(2).

(i) Category. \mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) is the category of finite-dimensional complex representations. This is a \mathbb{C}-linear rigid monoidal category. The G-action on tensor products is diagonal; on duals it is the contragredient.

(ii) Frobenius--Hopf object. A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) is the coordinate ring. Its Hopf structure encodes the group operations (see Table 1). The Frobenius pairing is positive definite.

(iii) Fibre functor. \tau \colon \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) \to \mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb{C}} is the forgetful functor. It is exact, faithful, and monoidal. By Tannaka--Krein duality, G \cong \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau).

(iv) Differential calculus. The left-invariant calculus on \mathrm{SU}(2) provides \Omega^1(A) = \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}. The universal derivation d \colon A \to \Omega^1(A) acts by df = \sum_i (\partial_i f) \omega_i.

(v) Braiding. In \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) the braiding is the flip c_{V,W}(v \otimes w) = w \otimes v, which is symmetric: c_{W,V} \circ c_{V,W} = \mathrm{id}. The first axiom asks for the ordering \prec_c that a braiding induces on the basis indexed by braid words. That ordering is well-founded for any braiding, the flip included, as the statement on braiding-induced orderings in the next chapter makes precise; non-symmetry c_{V,V}^{2} \neq \mathrm{id} is not used on words. So the example verifies all four axioms. What the flip lacks is non-symmetry on states: each crossing has order two, so exchange on states closes into chains. The example is the symmetric point of a one-parameter family whose braiding is not symmetric: the representation categories of the quantum deformation of \mathrm{SU}(2), constructed in the next chapter. On V \otimes V the braiding of a member of that family acts on the symmetric and antisymmetric parts by two scalars with product -1 whose ratio is not -1, so it satisfies a quadratic relation with two distinct roots and is not symmetric [kassel1995]. Items (i)--(iv) deform to the family with the same simple objects and the same Clebsch--Gordan rule, the Haar state h_A in place of the Haar measure, and the three-dimensional left-covariant calculus in place of the left-invariant forms; what changes away from the symmetric point is both the braiding, which for a generic member of the family has infinite order on states, and the trace symmetry on the quantised coordinate ring, where h_A ceases to vanish on commutators and becomes twisted by Woronowicz's modular Nakayama automorphism \nu (h_A(ab) = h_A(b\,\nu(a))) while untwisted trace symmetry persists on the Cartan weight centralizer and on ribbon traces of representations. In a suitable normalisation the deformed braiding is the flip plus a diagonal correction that vanishes at the symmetric point, which is the sense in which the symmetric example is the limit of the braided ones.

def:higher-forms:
Definition Higher differential forms. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe with differential calculus \Omega^1(A). The higher differential forms are the graded A-bimodule:

  \Omega^k(A) =  \bigwedge\nolimits_A^k \Omega^1(A), \qquad k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots

Here \Omega^0(A) = A. For an object V, \Lambda^k V denotes its k-th exterior power. The differential d \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+1}(A) extends the universal derivation by the graded Leibniz rule and satisfies d^2 = 0:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:de-rham-complex}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em]
  A = \Omega^0(A) \ar[r, "d"]
  & \Omega^1(A) \ar[r, "d"]
  & \Omega^2(A) \ar[r, "d"]
  & \cdots
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad (d^2 = 0)
\end{equation}
ex:higher-forms-su2:
Example Higher forms on \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). On A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)), the left-invariant calculus has \Omega^1(A) = \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}. The group is three-dimensional, so the exterior tower truncates at k = 3:

  • \Omega^0(A) = A
  • \Omega^1(A) = A \otimes \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}
  • \Omega^2(A) = A \otimes \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1 \wedge \omega_2, \omega_1 \wedge \omega_3, \omega_2 \wedge \omega_3\}
  • \Omega^3(A) = A \otimes \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1 \wedge \omega_2 \wedge \omega_3\}
  • \Omega^k(A) = 0 for k \geq 4.

The differential d is determined by d\omega_i = -\tfrac{1}{2} \epsilon_{ijk}\omega_j \wedge \omega_k.
sec:fundamental-object-explication:
The fundamental object and the emergent gauge group.

Two pieces of notation are fixed by the next two definitions: the fundamental object V — the self-dual simple object of categorical dimension 2 that tensor-generates \mathbf{C} — and the Tannaka dual G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau), the gauge group emergent from the fibre functor \tau.
def:fundamental-object:
Definition Fundamental object. Let \mathbf{C} be an R-linear rigid monoidal category. A fundamental object is an object V \in \mathbf{C} equipped with a volume form

  \epsilon \colon V \otimes V \longrightarrow \mathbf{1}

— the categorical determinant \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1} — together with an adjoint coform \eta \colon \mathbf{1} \to V \otimes V satisfying the two snake identities.
rem:fundamental-object-remark:
Remark The fundamental object under a fibre functor. The volume form \epsilon of a fundamental object, with its coform \eta, exhibits V as its own dual: a symplectic self-dual object, the datum that distinguishes \mathrm{SL}_2 / \mathrm{SU}(2) from \mathrm{GL}_2 [deligne1990].

Under a fibre functor the volume constraint forces \mathrm{rank}(V) = 2, so V is simple of categorical dimension 2: in \mathrm{SU}(2) it is V = V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2, every other simple object is an exterior or symmetric power of V, and V tensor-generates \mathbf{C} (the role of V is spelled out in a remark below).
def:tannaka-dual:
Definition Tannaka dual (emergent gauge group). Let \tau \colon \mathbf{C} \to R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod} be the fibre functor. A symmetry is a family of R-module automorphisms compatible with the tensor product — a monoidal natural automorphism of \tau. The Tannaka dual, or emergent gauge group,

  G \;=\; \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)

collects these families.
rem:tannaka-dual-remark: Remark The Tannaka dual as an emergent gauge group. The gauge group emerges from the pair (\mathbf{C}, \tau) alone. When (\mathbf{C}, \tau) is neutral Tannakian in the algebraic Tannakian formalism of Neantro Saavedra Rivano [saavedra-rivano1972] and Pierre Deligne [deligne1990], the Tannaka dual G is an affine group scheme over R and the reconstruction \mathbf{C} \simeq \mathrm{Rep}(G) holds.
rem:simple-objects-V:
Remark Simple objects and the role of V. Simple objects are the irreducible building blocks of a rigid monoidal category \mathbf{C}. An object X is simple if every monomorphism into X is zero or an isomorphism.

The faithful, exact functor \tau reflects simplicity: X is simple if and only if \tau(X) is a simple module. The fundamental object V is distinguished by two properties:

  1. Categorical dimension 2: \tau(V) is a rank-2 free module.
  2. Tensor generation: Every simple object appears as a direct summand of some tensor power V^{\otimes n}.
rem:unit-simplicity:
Remark Simplicity of the unit object and uniqueness of \epsilon. Choosing a specific volume form \epsilon fixes a fundamental unit of volume. The volume form is canonical up to a scalar because the unit object \mathbf{1} is simple.

The space of non-degenerate volume forms \mathrm{Hom}(\Lambda^2 V, \mathbf{1}) is one-dimensional over R. This follows because \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong R. Thus, any other non-degenerate epimorphism \epsilon' satisfies \epsilon' = c\epsilon for some unit c \in R^{\times}.

Once chosen, the gauge symmetries lock it in place. The volume \epsilon is a structural morphism intrinsic to the observable universe.
def:hochschild-homology:
Definition Hochschild homology. Let A be an associative algebra over a commutative ring R, and write A^{e} = A \otimes_R A^{\mathrm{op}} for its enveloping algebra, so that a bimodule over A is the same thing as a left module over A^{e}; A itself is one.

The Hochschild homology of A is the graded R-module

  HH_{n}(A) \;=\; \operatorname{Tor}^{A^{e}}_{n}(A, A), \qquad n \geq 0 .

It is computed by the Hochschild complex C_{n}(A) = A^{\otimes (n+1)} with the boundary

  b(a_0 \otimes a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n)
  = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (-1)^{i}\, a_0 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_i a_{i+1} \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n
  \;+\; (-1)^{n}\, a_n a_0 \otimes a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_{n-1},

whose last term wraps the tensor around: it is the cyclic structure of the complex, and the reason its homology deserves the name of a trace. The companion groups HH^{n}(A, M) = \operatorname{Ext}^{n}_{A^{e}}(A, M), for a bimodule M, are the Hochschild cohomology; HH^{n}(A) := HH^{n}(A, A), and it is HH^{2}(A, M) that classifies first-order deformations of the multiplication of A with values in M [weibel1994].

Degree zero. From the complex, HH_{0}(A) = A / [A, A], the quotient of A by the R-span of all commutators ab - ba; this is the cocenter of A. A symmetric trace \tau \colon A \to R with \tau(ab) = \tau(ba) vanishes on [A, A] and therefore factors through HH_{0}(A). Every untwisted trace in this paper --- the rigid ribbon trace of an endomorphism, the Markov trace of the later knot chapters on the Cartan weight centralizer, a character of a representation --- is a functional of this kind and depends only on the class in HH_0(A). When a Frobenius form is instead governed by a non-trivial Nakayama automorphism \nu, so that \psi(ab) = \psi(b\,\nu(a)) (as holds for the Haar state on the quantised coordinate ring of \mathrm{SU}(2) away from its symmetric point, where \psi does not vanish on [A, A]), \psi vanishes on twisted commutators ab - b\,\nu(a) and factors through the twisted degree-zero group HH_0(A, {}_\nu A) rather than HH_0(A).

Degree one. For A commutative, HH_{1}(A) = \Omega^{1}_{A/R}, the module of Kähler differentials: the class of a_0 \otimes a_1 goes to a_0\, da_1. For A smooth over a field of characteristic zero the pattern continues in every degree, HH_{n}(A) \cong \Omega^{n}_{A/R}; that is the Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg theorem, stated with its hypotheses in a later chapter. For a noncommutative A, such as the quantised coordinate ring of a group away from its classical point, no such identification is available, and the Hochschild homology and cohomology groups have to be computed directly [loday-1998, witherspoon2019].

Two conventions to keep apart. The definition above is for an algebra. For an R-linear category \mathbf{C} the same construction, with the objects of \mathbf{C} in place of the single algebra, gives the Hochschild homology of the category; in degree zero it is the direct sum over objects X of \operatorname{End}(X), modulo the relations fg = gf for every pair of morphisms f \colon X \to Y, g \colon Y \to X. It is this second object, written HH_{0}(\mathbf{C}), that is the target of the character map defined next.
def:grothendieck-group-of-a-qou:
Definition The Grothendieck group of a quantum universe. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe over the commutative ring R.

The Grothendieck group K_0(\mathbf{C}) is the abelian group generated by the isomorphism classes [X] of objects of \mathbf{C}, subject to the relations [X \oplus Y] = [X] + [Y].
rem:grothendieck-group-of-a-qou-remark:
Remark Block presentation, rank, quantum dimension and the fusion ring. The group K_0(\mathbf{C}) is the split Grothendieck group, the one appropriate to an additive category with no exact structure imposed; when \mathbf{C} is semisimple every short exact sequence splits and the two notions agree.

The block presentation. Axiom 4 of a quantum universe, Wedderburn semisimplicity, provides a finite set \widehat{A} of blocks and a simple object V_\lambda for each block \lambda, such that every object is a finite direct sum of the V_\lambda (simple objects). Hence

  K_0(\mathbf{C}) \;=\; \bigoplus_{\lambda \in \widehat{A}} \mathbb{Z}\,[V_\lambda] \;\cong\; \mathbb{Z}^{\widehat{A}},

a free abelian group on the blocks. Two homomorphisms out of it are used in the paper. The rank K_0(\mathbf{C}) \to \mathbb{Z} sends [V_\lambda] to 1, so it counts simple constituents. The quantum dimension of a rigid monoidal category, \dim_q(X) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{id}_X) \in \operatorname{End}(\mathbf{1}) = R, is additive under direct sums, so it extends to a homomorphism

  \dim_q \colon K_0(\mathbf{C}) \longrightarrow R, \qquad \sum_\lambda n_\lambda [V_\lambda] \longmapsto \sum_\lambda n_\lambda \dim_q(V_\lambda).

The ring structure. The tensor product of \mathbf{C} descends to K_0(\mathbf{C}), [X]\cdot[Y] = [X \otimes Y], because \otimes distributes over \oplus; with it K_0(\mathbf{C}) is a commutative ring when \mathbf{C} is braided, the fusion ring of \mathbf{C}, with unit [\mathbf{1}]. The quantum dimension is a ring homomorphism, since \dim_q(X \otimes Y) = \dim_q(X)\dim_q(Y) in a rigid braided category [kassel1995].
def:chern-character:
Definition The Chern character of a quantum universe. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe over R, with Grothendieck group K_0(\mathbf{C}) and degree-zero Hochschild homology HH_0(\mathbf{C}), the direct sum of the endomorphism modules of the objects modulo the relations fg = gf.

The Chern character of \mathbf{C} is the homomorphism

  \mathrm{ch} \colon K_0(\mathbf{C}) \longrightarrow HH_0(\mathbf{C}), \qquad [X] \longmapsto [\mathrm{id}_X],

sending the class of an object to the Hochschild class of its identity morphism. It is well defined because \mathrm{id}_{X \oplus Y} = \mathrm{id}_X \oplus \mathrm{id}_Y and the two summands are orthogonal, so [\mathrm{id}_{X \oplus Y}] = [\mathrm{id}_X] + [\mathrm{id}_Y] [bghl-2017].

The block presentation. By Wedderburn semisimplicity the central idempotents p_\lambda \in \operatorname{End}(A), one per block \lambda \in \widehat{A}, span HH_0(\mathbf{C}): every endomorphism of a simple object is a scalar, every object is a sum of simple ones, and morphisms between different blocks contribute nothing to the cocenter. So HH_0(\mathbf{C}) \cong R^{\widehat{A}}, spanned by the classes [p_\lambda] = [\mathrm{id}_{V_\lambda}], and in this basis

  \mathrm{ch}\Bigl(\sum_\lambda n_\lambda [V_\lambda]\Bigr) \;=\; \sum_\lambda n_\lambda\, [p_\lambda] \;=\; (n_\lambda)_{\lambda \in \widehat{A}} .

The Chern character is therefore the map \mathbb{Z}^{\widehat{A}} \to R^{\widehat{A}} induced by the ring map \mathbb{Z} \to R: injective when R has characteristic zero, and in every case an isomorphism after tensoring with R.

The factorisation of the quantum dimension. The rigid trace \mathrm{tr} \colon \operatorname{End}(X) \to \operatorname{End}(\mathbf{1}) = R of a rigid monoidal category satisfies \mathrm{tr}(fg) = \mathrm{tr}(gf), so it descends to a linear map

  \mathrm{ev} \colon HH_0(\mathbf{C}) \longrightarrow R, \qquad \mathrm{ev}[p_\lambda] = \dim_q(V_\lambda),

and the quantum dimension on K_0(\mathbf{C}) is the composite

  K_0(\mathbf{C}) \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{ch}\ } HH_0(\mathbf{C}) \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{ev}\ } R, \qquad \dim_q = \mathrm{ev} \circ \mathrm{ch}.

The factorisation holds on all of K_0(\mathbf{C}), because both sides are additive and they agree on each generator [V_\lambda]. Its content is a separation of roles: the Chern character records which simple constituents an object has and how many times, an integer datum independent of the deformation; the evaluation records what the trace assigns to each block, which is where the deformation enters. A quantum dimension is one number obtained from the whole character by one evaluation — for the group \mathrm{SU}(2), the evaluation at the pivotal element of a Laurent polynomial whose evaluation at 1 is the ordinary dimension, as the next example makes explicit. It is not itself an Euler characteristic of anything, and the base curve's Euler characteristic, which is an alternating sum over all the Hochschild degrees of a different object, is not obtained from it.
sec:qu-consequences-intro:
This section reads off the consequences of the QU axioms and the Frobenius pairing. In \mathrm{SU}(2), the coordinate ring \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) carries a comultiplication built from the group-multiplication rule. The involution is the conjugate-transpose adjoint on \mathbf{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). These structures are categorical; they follow directly from the Frobenius pairing.

First, the Frobenius relation. The comultiplication \Delta_\mu dual to \mu under the Frobenius pairing satisfies (\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu) = \Delta_\mu \circ \mu. The \mathrm{SU}(2) picture verifies this identity on \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). Second, the involutive \ast-structure: a contravariant endofunctor \dagger assembled from the antipode and the Frobenius form. Its positivity—where f^{\dagger} \circ f is positive in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1})—is the categorical analogue of the C^*-axiom.

Three observations place these results in context. The symbols \dagger, \ast, and the physicist's adjoint denote distinct structures. Tannaka--Krein duality lets the fibre functor \tau reconstruct the group itself. Finally, the QU axioms are independent over arbitrary rings.
prop:frobenius-relation:
Proposition Frobenius relation. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe. Denote by \Delta_\mu the comultiplication on A dual to \mu under the Frobenius pairing. This compatibility makes A a Frobenius algebra. The Frobenius relation holds:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:frobenius-relation}
\begin{gathered}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3.5em]
  A \otimes A
    \ar[r, "\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu"]
    \ar[d, "\mu"']
  & A \otimes A \otimes A
    \ar[d, "\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}"]
  \\
  A \ar[r, "\Delta_\mu"']
  & A \otimes A
\end{tikzcd}
\\[-0.5em]
\text{\small Frobenius relation: } (\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu) = \Delta_\mu \circ \mu
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}

Sliding a multiplication past a comultiplication yields the same result as composing them.
prf:frobenius-relation:
Proof Proof of Frobenius relation. The Frobenius form \int_A and the multiplication \mu together define a non-degenerate pairing \langle a, b \rangle = \int_A(\mu(a \otimes b)) (Frobenius pairing). Non-degeneracy gives a copairing \gamma = \sum_i \gamma_i' \otimes \gamma_i'' \in A \otimes A, the unique element satisfying the snake identity \sum_i \langle a, \gamma_i' \rangle\, \gamma_i'' = a for all a \in A. The comultiplication dual to \mu under the pairing is

  \Delta_\mu = (\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \gamma),
  \qquad
  \Delta_\mu(b) = \sum_i \mu(b \otimes \gamma_i') \otimes \gamma_i'' .

That this map is the transpose of \mu under the pairing is the standard equivalence of the two descriptions of the comultiplication of a Frobenius algebra ([kock2004], §2.3); it uses only the snake identity.

With this form the relation is associativity. For a, b \in A,

  (\mu \otimes \mathrm{id})\bigl(a \otimes \Delta_\mu(b)\bigr)
  = \sum_i \mu\bigl(a \otimes \mu(b \otimes \gamma_i')\bigr) \otimes \gamma_i''
  = \sum_i \mu\bigl(\mu(a \otimes b) \otimes \gamma_i'\bigr) \otimes \gamma_i''
  = \Delta_\mu\bigl(\mu(a \otimes b)\bigr).

Hence (\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu) = \Delta_\mu \circ \mu. \square
ex:frobenius-relation-su2:
Example The Frobenius relation in \mathrm{SU}(2). The Frobenius relation is checked here for A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)).

Setup. A carries pointwise multiplication \mu(f \otimes g) = f \cdot g. The comultiplication \Delta_\mu dual to \mu under the Haar Frobenius pairing \langle f, g \rangle = \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} f g is the diagonal comultiplication, characterised by

\langle \Delta_\mu(f),\, g \otimes h \rangle = \langle f,\, g h \rangle = \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} f\, g\, h .

Equivalently \Delta_\mu(f)(x, y) = f(x)\,\delta_{x = y}: it is supported on the diagonal — a distribution for the continuous group, a genuine element of A \otimes A for any finite group. Note that \Delta_\mu is not the Hopf group-comultiplication f \mapsto f(xy); that map is a bialgebra structure, not the Frobenius comultiplication dual to \mu.

Concrete verification. Evaluate both sides of (\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu) = \Delta_\mu \circ \mu on f, h \in A.

  • Left side. (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu)(f \otimes h)(x, y, z) = f(x)\, h(y)\, \delta_{y = z}. Applying \mu \otimes \mathrm{id} multiplies the first two tensor factors (x = y), giving (f \cdot h)(x)\, \delta_{x = z}.
  • Right side. \Delta_\mu(\mu(f \otimes h))(x, z) = \Delta_\mu(f \cdot h)(x, z) = (f \cdot h)(x)\, \delta_{x = z}.

Both sides equal (f \cdot h)(x)\, \delta_{x = z}, so the Frobenius relation holds.

Interpretation. The diagonal comultiplication records a function together with the constraint that its two output copies coincide. Multiplying two functions and then duplicating along the diagonal gives the same diagonal-supported element as duplicating one factor first and then multiplying — the compatibility of \mu with the pairing-dual \Delta_\mu that makes A a Frobenius algebra.
def:involutive-structure:
Definition Involutive structure (\ast-structure). Let (\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1}) be an R-linear rigid monoidal category. An involutive structure on \mathbf{C} is a contravariant endofunctor \dagger \colon \mathbf{C}^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathbf{C} satisfying:

  1. Identity on objects: X^{\dagger} = X.

  2. Involutivity: f^{\dagger\dagger} = f:

    \begin{equation}\label{eq:involutivity-cd}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5em]
  X \ar[r, bend left=30, "f = f^{\dagger\dagger}"]
  & Y \ar[l, bend left=30, "f^{\dagger}"]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

  3. Monoidal compatibility: (\mathrm{id}_X \otimes f)^{\dagger} = \mathrm{id}_X \otimes f^{\dagger}:

    \begin{equation}\label{eq:monoidal-dagger-cd}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  X \otimes Y \ar[r, "\mathrm{id} \otimes f"]
    \ar[d, "(\mathrm{id} \otimes f)^{\dagger}"']
  & X \otimes Z \ar[d, "\mathrm{id} \otimes f^{\dagger}"] \\
  X \otimes Z \ar[r, equal]
  & X \otimes Z
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

  4. Contravariance: (g \circ f)^{\dagger} = f^{\dagger} \circ g^{\dagger}:

    \begin{equation}\label{eq:dagger-contravariance}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em]
  X \ar[r, "f"] & Y \ar[r, "g"] & Z
\end{tikzcd}
\quad\xmapsto{\dagger}\quad
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em]
  Z \ar[r, "g^{\dagger}"] & Y \ar[r, "f^{\dagger}"] & X
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
ex:involutive-structure-example: Example The antipode as an involutive structure. For the Hopf algebra A in a quantum universe, the antipode S provides an involutive structure via f^{\dagger} = \int_A \circ \mu(S(f) \otimes -).
prop:positive-definite-dagger:
Proposition Frobenius dagger is positive-definite. A positive-definite dagger gives categorical states genuine squared lengths. Let (\mathbf{C}, A) be a quantum universe whose endomorphism ring \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong R is an ordered field. Assume a Frobenius pairing with form \int_A, and an antipode S that is R-linear, involutive (S^2 = \mathrm{id}), anti-multiplicative (S(xy) = S(y)\,S(x)) and unital.

For a morphism f \colon \mathbf{1} \to A define the Frobenius dagger

  f^{\dagger} =  \int_A \circ\, \mu(S(f) \otimes -),

and the form h(f, g) = \int_A \mu(S(f) \otimes g), so that f^{\dagger} \circ f = h(f, f). Assume that h is positive definite: h(f, f) > 0 for every non-zero f \colon \mathbf{1} \to A. Write L_x for left multiplication by x \in A. Then:

  1. L_{S(x)} is the unique R-linear adjoint of L_x for h, that is h(L_x a, b) = h(a, L_{S(x)} b);
  2. the dagger L_x^{\dagger} = L_{S(x)} is involutive and reverses products on these operators, as an involutive structure requires; this is checked only on left multiplications: L_x^{\dagger\dagger} = L_x and (L_x L_y)^{\dagger} = L_y^{\dagger} L_x^{\dagger};
  3. on \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong R the dagger is S, which is the identity there;
  4. f^{\dagger} \circ f > 0 for every non-zero f \colon \mathbf{1} \to A.

Item 4 is the positivity hypothesis on h read through f^{\dagger} \circ f = h(f, f). Requiring S to be R-linear and involutive restricts this formulation to formally real ordered scalar fields at the involutive point: over \mathbb{C}, R-linearity would give h(if, if) = -h(f, f) < 0, and on the coordinate algebra of \mathrm{SU}(2) and its non-involutive quantum deformations (S^2 \neq \mathrm{id}_A) one already has \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} S(\beta)\beta = 0. Over \mathbb{C} and for non-involutive Hopf \ast-algebras, the positive GNS dagger replaces S with a conjugate-linear \ast-involution a \mapsto a^* (satisfying (S \circ *)^2 = \mathrm{id}_A) and sesquilinear form h_*(f, g) = \int_A f^* g.
prf:positive-definite-dagger:
Proof Proof that the Frobenius dagger is positive-definite. Write h(f, g) = \int_A \mu(S(f) \otimes g) and L_x for left multiplication by x \in A.

Adjoint of L_x. Since S is anti-multiplicative, S(x a) = S(a)\,S(x), so

  h(L_x a, b) = \int_A \mu\bigl(S(a)\,S(x) \otimes b\bigr)
  = \int_A \mu\bigl(S(a) \otimes S(x)\, b\bigr) = h(a, L_{S(x)} b).

Uniqueness. If U is R-linear with h(L_x a, b) = h(a, U b) for all a, b, put c = U b - S(x) b. Then h(c, c) = h(c, U b) - h(c, S(x) b) = h(L_x c, b) - h(L_x c, b) = 0, so c = 0 by positive definiteness.

Involution and contravariance. Applying the adjoint formula to S(x) gives h(L_{S(x)} a, b) = h(a, L_{S^2(x)} b) = h(a, L_x b), using S^2 = \mathrm{id}. Applying it to x y gives h(L_{xy} a, b) = h(a, L_{S(y)} L_{S(x)} b), using S(xy) = S(y)\,S(x). The involution S^2 = \mathrm{id} is a hypothesis: for a pivotal Hopf algebra S^2 is conjugation by the pivotal element, which is the identity only in the involutory case.

Scalars. For r \in R, S(r \cdot 1) = r\,S(1) = r \cdot 1, so on \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong R the dagger is S and fixes every scalar.

Positivity. f^{\dagger} \circ f = \int_A \mu(S(f) \otimes f) = h(f, f), which is positive for f \neq 0 by hypothesis. \square

Positivity does not follow from non-degeneracy of the pairing: a non-degenerate form can have isotropic vectors. On R^2 the form \langle x, y\rangle = x_1 y_2 + x_2 y_1 is non-degenerate and \langle e_1, e_1\rangle = 0. The positivity of h is therefore an input, as in the GNS construction, where it is the positivity of the state ([kock2004], Ch. 2, for the Frobenius side); over \mathbb{C} and on non-involutive Hopf \ast-algebras where S^2 \neq \mathrm{id}_A, the same proof applies verbatim with S replaced by the conjugate-linear \ast-involution x \mapsto x^* in h_*(a, b) = \int_A a^* b, using (x^*)^* = x in place of S^2 = \mathrm{id}_A and r^* \cdot 1_A on scalars.
ex:positive-dagger-su2:
Example Positive-definite dagger in \mathrm{SU}(2). Positive-definiteness is checked here in \mathbf{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)).

The dagger involution. On \mathbf{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)), the dagger sends f \colon V \to W to its conjugate transpose f^\dagger = \bar{f}^{T} \colon W \to V.

Positive-definiteness on V = \mathbb{C}^2. The fundamental representation V = \mathbb{C}^2 carries the standard Hermitian inner product \langle v, w \rangle = v^\dagger w. The \mathrm{SU}(2)-action preserves this inner product.

For any endomorphism f \colon V \to V, the composite f^\dagger f satisfies:

\langle f^\dagger f  v, v \rangle = \| f v \|^2 \geq 0.

Thus f^\dagger f has real non-negative eigenvalues. By Schur's lemma, f = \lambda \mathrm{id}, forcing f^\dagger f = |\lambda|^2 \mathrm{id}.

Interpretation. Positive-definiteness makes \mathbf{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) a C^*-tensor category. This is the categorical shadow of the compactness of \mathrm{SU}(2).
rem:dagger-notation:
Remark Notation: \dagger, \ast, and the physicist's adjoint. Three notations for "adjoint" coexist:

  • f^{\dagger} denotes the Frobenius adjoint: the involution derived from the Frobenius pairing. This is the categorical structure.
  • f^{\ast} denotes complex conjugation. On \mathcal{O}(G), it acts as f^{\ast}(g) = \overline{f(g)}.
  • A^{\dagger}_{\mathrm{phys}} denotes the physicist's adjoint on a Hilbert space.

In the categorical setting, only \dagger is defined.
rem:tannaka-krein-overview:
Remark Tannaka--Krein duality: what the fibre functor gives us. Tannaka--Krein duality recovers the gauge group from the fibre functor \tau. It comprises four statements:

  1. Reconstruction. The group G emerges from \tau: G \cong \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau).
  2. Equivalence. The functor \tau establishes a monoidal equivalence \mathbf{C} \simeq \mathrm{Rep}(G).
  3. Rigidity. Any two fibre functors are isomorphic, reconstructing the same group up to inner automorphism.
  4. Constraint propagation. Algebraic conditions on \tau propagate to G. The volume constraint cuts the automorphism group from \mathrm{GL} down to \mathrm{SL}.

Origin of the deformation parameter. The deformation parameter enters categorically: when the braiding c_{V,V} is non-symmetric, the parameter is its eigenvalue on S^2 V, and Woronowicz's reconstruction recovers the quantum deformation of \mathrm{SU}(2) at that value. This fixes what the parameter is, not what it equals — the braiding is assumed data, so its eigenvalue is determined by the assumption rather than by anything upstream of it. Chapter 2 extracts the parameter from the braiding; its numerical value is the CAL-2 calibration, not a categorical consequence.
rem:axiom-independence:
Remark Independence of the QU axioms. Are the four axioms of a quantum universe independent?

Temporal braiding. Over a characteristic-zero field, Deligne's theorem shows every symmetric monoidal category admits a fibre functor. Only a braiding is required, and only over a commutative ring, so no fibre functor is supplied. The braiding axiom is independent of the fibre functor.

Frobenius--Hopf. A general Hopf algebra need not carry a non-degenerate Frobenius form. The Frobenius condition A \cong A^{\vee} is strictly stronger than the Hopf axioms.

Symmetric Frobenius. A Frobenius algebra need not be symmetric: the left and right traces induced by a non-symmetric form differ by the Nakayama automorphism, which is trivial exactly when the form is symmetric. The axiom is therefore a genuine restriction on the Frobenius--Hopf datum, not a consequence of it.

Wedderburn semisimplicity. A Frobenius object need not be semisimple: a truncated polynomial algebra k[x]/(x^n) carries a non-degenerate Frobenius form and is local, hence has a single block and a nilpotent radical. Semisimplicity is therefore independent of the preceding three axioms. It is the assumption that does the work later: given it, the co-Casimir trace identity, proved in the mass-theory chapter, follows by linearity over the central idempotents rather than being assumed.

The differential calculus \Omega^1(A) is a separate matter. For smooth algebraic groups Kähler differentials exist automatically, but for quantum groups away from the classical point a differential calculus need not exist or be unique, so its existence is an assumption rather than a theorem.

In full generality, all four axioms are independent.
sec:qu-structures-intro:
This section assembles the differential-geometric vocabulary; Quantum Observable Universes later equips it with observability and measurability. A connection with its curvature, the jet object packaging its first-order data, a Hodge star, and an internal Poisson structure comprise this vocabulary.

The connection comes first because everything else refines it. A connection is a morphism \nabla \colon A \to A \otimes \Omega^1(A) satisfying the Leibniz rule, with curvature F_\nabla = \nabla^2 \colon A \to A \otimes \Omega^2(A). Every QU admits such a \nabla. The space of connections is an affine space over \Omega^1(A) \otimes \mathrm{Ad}(A). On \mathrm{SU}(2), the flat left-invariant connection \varTheta = g^{-1} dg makes the abstract object concrete. The first-order data of the connection packages into the jet object J^1(A) = A \otimes_{\mathbf{C}} \Omega^1(A), the middle term of the universal extension 0 \to A \otimes \Omega^1(A) \to J^1(A) \to A \to 0.

The Hodge half runs in parallel. The categorical Hodge star \star \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{n-k}(A) is defined by \alpha \wedge \star \beta = \int_A(\alpha^* \cdot \beta) \mathrm{vol}. It uses the Frobenius form, the antipode-conjugate, and a normalised volume form. The operator is well-defined and satisfies \star^2 = \mathrm{id}. On the three-dimensional left-invariant calculus of \mathrm{SU}(2), it sends a 1-form to a 2-form by \star\omega_i = \tfrac12 \epsilon_{ijk} \omega_j \wedge \omega_k, recovering the classical correspondence.

An internal Poisson structure links the differential calculus to deformation theory. The internal Poisson object defines a Poisson bivector as a morphism \pi \colon \mathbf{1} \to \Lambda^2(\Omega^1(A)^{\vee}) subject to the Schouten--Nijenhuis Jacobi condition [\pi, \pi]_{\mathrm{SN}} = 0 and a biderivation Leibniz rule. The bracket is \{f, g\} = \langle \pi, df \wedge dg \rangle. This bivector \pi is the image of the Hochschild--Kostant--Rosenberg map applied to the first-order Hopf deformation. It matches the internal Poisson bracket against the skew-Poisson structure of formal-group integration.
def:categorical-connection:
Definition Categorical connection and curvature. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe over R with differential forms \Omega^k(A) (higher forms).

A categorical connection on A is a morphism \nabla \colon A \to A \otimes \Omega^1(A) in \mathbf{C} satisfying the Leibniz rule \nabla(\mu(a \otimes b)) = \nabla(a) \cdot b + a \cdot \nabla(b). The rule is expressed by the commutativity of the Leibniz triangle:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:leibniz-triangle}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3.5em]
  A \otimes A
    \ar[r, "\mu"]
    \ar[dr, "{\nabla \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes \nabla}"']
  & A \ar[d, "\nabla"]
  \\
  & A \otimes \Omega^1(A)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

The curvature of \nabla is the composition:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:curvature-composition}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em]
  A \ar[r, "\nabla"]
  & A \otimes \Omega^1(A) \ar[r, "\nabla"]
  & A \otimes \Omega^2(A)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

This composition is denoted F_\nabla = \nabla^2.
rem:categorical-connection-remark: Remark Classical connections and A-linearity of curvature. A categorical connection generalizes the classical de Rham connection d; the \mathrm{SU}(2) instance in Example gives a concrete picture. Its curvature F_\nabla = \nabla^2 is A-linear, a standard consequence of the Leibniz rule.
prop:categorical-connection-exists:
Proposition Existence of categorical connections. A categorical connection equips the observable algebra A with a covariant-derivative structure. The abstract triple carries the same differential geometry as a bundle with connection. Here \Omega^1(A) plays the role of one-forms, and \nabla sends an observable to its differential.

Every quantum universe (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) admits a categorical connection, which is a morphism \nabla \colon A \to \Omega^1(A) satisfying the Leibniz rule. Uniqueness up to gauge is the next proposition.
prf:categorical-connection-exists: Proof Proof of existence of categorical connections. Witness: the trivial connection \nabla_0 = d, where d is the de Rham differential of the Kähler module \Omega^1(A). The Leibniz rule d(ab) = (da)b + a(db) is part of the differential- calculus axiom of the QU.
prop:categorical-connection-unique:
Proposition Uniqueness of categorical connections (up to gauge). Two categorical connections \nabla_1, \nabla_2 on the same QU differ by a \mathrm{Ad}(A)-valued 1-form:

  \nabla_2 - \nabla_1 \;\in\; \Omega^1(A) \otimes \mathrm{Ad}(A).

This difference is a categorical gauge potential. The space of connections is an affine space over \Omega^1(A) \otimes \mathrm{Ad}(A), making uniqueness hold up to gauge.
prf:categorical-connection-unique:
Proof Proof of uniqueness of categorical connections up to gauge. Uniqueness up to gauge follows once the difference of two connections is shown to be a derivation, hence lies in a fixed module. To that end, consider the difference \omega = \nabla_2 - \nabla_1, which is R-linear: for any a, b \in A the Leibniz rule applied to both \nabla_1 and \nabla_2 gives

  \omega(ab)
  \;=\; \nabla_2(ab) - \nabla_1(ab)
  \;=\; \bigl(\nabla_2(a)\,b + a\,\nabla_2(b)\bigr)
        - \bigl(\nabla_1(a)\,b + a\,\nabla_1(b)\bigr)
  \;=\; \omega(a)\,b + a\,\omega(b).

This shows \omega is a derivation, i.e. an element of \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(A, \Omega^1(A))^{\text{Leibniz}} \cong \Omega^1(A) \otimes \mathrm{Ad}(A) via the \mathrm{Ad}(A)-twisted 1-form correspondence. Connections therefore form an affine space over this module; uniqueness is up to gauge translation within this affine structure.
ex:categorical-connection-su2:
Example Categorical connection as Maurer--Cartan form on \mathrm{SU}(2). The categorical connection is instantiated here on SU(2).

Classical setup. A connection on a Lie group G is a \mathfrak{g}-valued 1-form on G. The canonical choice is the Maurer--Cartan form \varTheta = g^{-1} dg, a left-invariant \mathfrak{su}(2)-valued 1-form.

Explicit matrix form. For g \in \mathrm{SU}(2) written as

g = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha & -\bar{\beta} \\ \beta & \bar{\alpha} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad |\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1,

the inverse is g^{-1} = g^\dagger = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} \bar{\alpha} & \bar{\beta} \\ -\beta & \alpha \end{smallmatrix}\bigr). The Maurer--Cartan form evaluates to:

\varTheta = g^{-1} dg
= \begin{pmatrix}
\bar{\alpha}  d\alpha + \bar{\beta}  d\beta &
\bar{\alpha}  d(-\bar{\beta}) + \bar{\beta}  d\bar{\alpha} \\
-\beta  d\alpha + \alpha  d\beta &
-\beta  d(-\bar{\beta}) + \alpha  d\bar{\alpha}
\end{pmatrix}.

Using the constraint \alpha d\bar{\alpha} + \bar{\alpha} d\alpha + \beta d\bar{\beta} + \bar{\beta} d\beta = 0, one verifies that \varTheta is traceless and skew-Hermitian: \varTheta \in \Omega^1(G; \mathfrak{su}(2)).

Flatness. The curvature of the Maurer--Cartan form is F = d\varTheta + \varTheta \wedge \varTheta. The Maurer--Cartan equation states that F = 0 identically. This follows from d(g^{-1}) = -g^{-1} (dg) g^{-1}:

d\varTheta = d(g^{-1} dg) = d(g^{-1}) \wedge dg
= -g^{-1} dg \wedge g^{-1} dg = -\varTheta \wedge \varTheta,

so F = d\varTheta + \varTheta \wedge \varTheta = 0. The Maurer--Cartan form is a flat connection.

Categorical interpretation. The connection \varTheta corresponds to the natural transformation implementing parallel transport in \mathbf{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). Flatness (F = 0) means parallel transport around any contractible loop is trivial. Since \mathrm{SU}(2) \cong S^3 is connected, all monodromy is trivial. The Maurer--Cartan connection has trivial holonomy.
def:categorical-jet:
Definition Categorical jet object. A jet object packages an element of A together with its infinitesimal variation. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe over a commutative ring R with connection \nabla (categorical connection), and assume A is commutative, so that I = \ker(\mu \colon A \otimes A \to A) is an ideal of A \otimes A. The jet object is the first-jet module

  J^1(A) := (A \otimes A)/I^2 .

The section \ell(a) = [a \otimes 1] and the left inverse r \colon J^1(A) \to A induced by \mu satisfy r \circ \ell = \mathrm{id}_A, and \ker r = I/I^2, which is the module \Omega^1_{A/R} of Kähler differentials. The jet object therefore fits into the split extension

\begin{equation}\label{eq:jet-ses}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em]
  0 \ar[r]
  & \Omega^1_{A/R} \ar[r]
  & J^1(A) \ar[r, "j^1"]
  & A \ar[r]
  & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

where j^1 = r is the jet evaluation.
def:categorical-hodge-star:
Definition Categorical Hodge star. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe over R with higher differential forms \Omega^k(A) (higher forms). The categorical Hodge star is the involution \star \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{n-k}(A) defined by

  \alpha \wedge \star \beta
  = \int_A\!\bigl(\alpha^* \cdot \beta\bigr) \mathrm{vol},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:categorical-hodge-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "\star"] \ar[d, "\star"']
  & \Omega^{n-k}(A) \ar[d, "\star"] \\
  \Omega^{n-k}(A) \ar[r, equal]
  & \Omega^{n-k}(A)
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad (\star^2 = \mathrm{id})
\end{equation}

where \int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1} is the Frobenius form, \alpha^* = S(\alpha) is the antipode-conjugate, and \mathrm{vol} \in \Omega^n(A) is the volume form (the unique invariant top form normalised by \int_A(\mathrm{vol}) = 1).
rem:categorical-hodge-star-remark: Remark Involutivity of the categorical Hodge star. That \star^2 = \mathrm{id} follows from the non-degeneracy of \int_A and the involutivity of the antipode. The extension of \star to \Omega^k(A) follows from the graded Leibniz rule for S.
prop:categorical-hodge-star-exists: Proposition Existence of the categorical Hodge star. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe of dimension n with volume form \mathrm{vol} \in \Omega^n(A). The categorical Hodge star \star \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{n-k}(A) exists as a morphism in \mathbf{C} and satisfies \star^2 = \mathrm{id}. Uniqueness is the next proposition.
prf:categorical-hodge-star-exists: Proof Proof of existence of the categorical Hodge star. Non-degeneracy of the Frobenius pairing (Frobenius pairing) gives a unique morphism \star \beta \in \Omega^{n-k}(A) for every \beta \in \Omega^k(A) determined by the defining identity \alpha \wedge \star \beta = \int_A(\alpha^* \cdot \beta) \mathrm{vol} for all \alpha \in \Omega^k(A). Involutivity \star^2 = \mathrm{id} follows from S^2 = \mathrm{id} on the commutative Frobenius--Hopf algebra A, extended to \Omega^k(A) via the graded Leibniz rule.
